lead: The metaverse is a persistent, shared, synchronous 3D layer over the internet. Persistent means the world keeps its state when you leave. Synchronous means all users see the same moment. Shared means one coordinate space for everyone. XR trends are the hardware and network steps that make this layer wearable and always on: lighter glasses, on-device tracking, edge rendering, and open standards. You meet it in shared design reviews, remote machine support, and training rooms where a phone or headset shows the same anchored object to two people.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the AR requirements, 6.5 for interaction, and Unit 1 for the XR definitions.

blocks.text: A metaverse is not any VR app. A single-player game has a world, but no shared state with other users. A video call has shared state, but no 3D space. The term needs these properties together.

items: Persistence: the world and its objects keep their state when a user disconnects. A meeting room keeps the notes on the table.
Synchrony: every user sees the same event at the same time, within the network delay.
Shared space: one coordinate system and one set of anchors, so a virtual chair is in the same place for every device.
Avatars and identity: each user has a body or pointer and a stable identity.
Economy: optional but common; users can own, buy, or sell items.
Interoperability: the same identity, content, and avatar can move between devices and apps.

blocks.text: These properties explain why the metaverse is a layer, not a product. A factory in Pune runs a digital twin of a line; a digital twin is a live model of a real asset. An engineer in Chennai puts an anchor on valve V-12. A second engineer in Delhi opens the same anchor and sees the same label. The world persists after both log out. That is a small metaverse service.

sections.h3: The stack from devices to experience

blocks.text: The figure shows the working stack. Read from the bottom. Devices and hardware are phones, headsets, and glasses. Network and cloud carry data and store the shared map. Standards and identity let an app run on different devices and keep one account. 3D engine and rendering draws frames; a cloud renderer may do this on a server. Platform and world keeps accounts and shared state. Experience and content is the game, meeting, or training task.

The AR cloud is the shared map in the network layer. A device builds a local map with SLAM (see 6.3). It sends selected feature points to the cloud. The cloud merges them into a world map. A spatial anchor is a named pose in that map: a position and an orientation. Device A creates an anchor at a real valve and stores the anchor ID. Device B localises itself in the same map, reads the ID, and places its label at the same pose. Both devices now agree on the same real point.

WebXR is a browser API for XR. A page asks for an XR session; the browser talks to the device. A link opens AR or VR without an app install. This lowers the cost of a shared session, but browser and device must support the same features.

sections.h3: Cloud rendering and the latency budget

blocks.text: A headset must answer head motion fast. Motion-to-photon latency is the time from a head movement to the display changing. Above about 20 ms, many users feel lag and nausea. The budget splits into rendering, network, and display scan.

blocks.where: t<sub>total</sub> is motion-to-photon latency in ms; t<sub>render</sub> is frame draw time; t<sub>network</sub> is round-trip network time; t<sub>scan</sub> is display scan-out time.

blocks.text: On-device rendering keeps t<sub>network</sub> small. Cloud rendering moves the GPU to a server, which helps thin glasses, but the network term grows. Light in fibre travels at about 2 × 10⁸ m per second, so distance sets a hard lower bound. A server 1000 km away adds 10 ms of round-trip light time before switching or queueing. Edge computing puts the server in a nearby data centre, often in the same city. 5G and Wi-Fi 6/7 reduce the radio part but cannot beat the speed of light.

sections.h3: Hardware, standards and a realistic view

blocks.text: Glasses trends: waveguides are thin glass plates that guide light from a small projector to the eye, so the display can look like ordinary glasses. Micro-LED and laser scanning are small, bright light engines. Pancake optics fold the light path with polarising films, so a headset becomes thinner. Colour passthrough uses cameras to show the real world in colour on a mixed-reality headset. Eye tracking and hand tracking remove controllers for some tasks, and SLAM on the device removes external cameras.

Standards: OpenXR is an application interface; one app can talk to many headsets and runtimes. glTF and USDZ are 3D content formats; a model in either can be shown by many viewers. These standards reduce porting work, but they do not make every world interoperable.

Challenges are real. Always-on cameras raise privacy problems. Shared spaces need safety rules and moderation. Headsets cost money, and cloud rendering uses energy. Accessibility is incomplete: small text, weight, and battery life exclude users. The digital divide matters when a school cannot buy headsets. Near term, phone AR and light glasses give guidance, translation, and remote help; they will not replace every screen.

figure.caption: Each lane spends the same 20 ms motion-to-photon budget, in milliseconds. Rendering takes 8 ms and the display scan 4 ms, so the network gets only 8 ms; a server 1000 km away needs 10 ms of light time, and the total becomes 22 ms, which is 2 ms over the budget.

spec.aria: Two timelines in milliseconds: the 20 ms budget splits into 8 ms render, 8 ms network and 4 ms scan, while a server 1000 km away needs 10 ms of network, giving 22 ms total and overshooting the budget.

examples.question: A cloud-rendered XR system allows 20 ms from head motion to the photon leaving the display. Rendering takes 8 ms and the display scan takes 4 ms. (a) What network round-trip budget is left? (b) Light in fibre travels at about 2 × 10⁸ m per second. What is the maximum one-way distance to the server? (c) A server is 1000 km away. Find the round-trip light time and the total latency. Does it meet the budget?
steps: 2. Round-trip distance in 8 ms: d = c t = (2 × 10⁸ m/s)(8 × 10⁻³ s) = 1.6 × 10⁶ m = 1600 km.
4. For 1000 km, one-way distance = 10⁶ m; round trip = 2 × 10⁶ m.
5. Round-trip time = d ÷ c = (2 × 10⁶ m) ÷ (2 × 10⁸ m/s) = 0.01 s = 10 ms.
6. Total latency = 10 + 8 + 4 = 22 ms. This is 2 ms over the 20 ms budget.
examples.answer: The network budget is 8 ms, the maximum one-way distance is 800 km, and the 1000 km server gives 22 ms total, so it misses the budget by 2 ms.
examples.check:
budget = 20
render = 8
scan = 4
net_budget = budget - render - scan
print(int(net_budget))
c = 2e8
t_net = net_budget / 1000.0
d_round = t_net * c
print(int(round(d_round / 1000.0)))
print(int(round(d_round / 2000.0)))
dist_km = 1000
d_one = dist_km * 1000.0
t_round = (2 * d_one) / c
print(int(round(t_round * 1000.0)))
total = render + scan + t_round * 1000.0
print(int(round(total)))
print(int(round(total - budget)))

traps: Calling any VR game 'the metaverse'. A metaverse needs persistence and shared state across users and devices; a single-player game has neither.
Using one-way distance as the network time. The latency budget usually uses a round trip; double the one-way light time.
Confusing a spatial anchor with a marker. A marker is a printed image tracked by the camera; a spatial anchor is a pose in a shared map.
Giving a fixed date for full AR glasses. Near-term products are phone AR and light guidance glasses, not every promised feature.
Mixing OpenXR and glTF. OpenXR is the app-to-runtime interface; glTF is a 3D content format.

quiz.q: Define persistence and synchrony for a metaverse.
quiz.a: Persistence: the world keeps state after a user leaves. Synchrony: all users see the same event at the same time within network delay.

quiz.q: Why is a single-player VR game not a metaverse?
quiz.a: It has no shared state or synchrony with other users, and it does not persist as a shared world across devices.

quiz.q: A budget is 18 ms. Rendering takes 7 ms and display scan 3 ms. Find the network round-trip budget.
Light in fibre is 2 × 10⁸ m/s. A network budget is 6 ms. Find the maximum one-way distance.
quiz.a: Round trip = 2×10⁸ × 6×10⁻³ = 1.2×10⁶ m = 1200 km; one way = 600 km.

quiz.q: Why does cloud XR push servers to the edge?
quiz.a: Fibre delay grows with distance. A distant server uses the network budget and misses motion-to-photon latency; an edge server cuts round-trip distance and time.
It is an application interface that lets one XR app talk to different headsets and runtimes.

quiz.q: Two devices must share a spatial anchor. What steps must each device do?
quiz.a: Build or load the same world map, localise to it, read the anchor pose or ID, and place content at that pose. Both then use the same coordinates.

quiz.q: Name two privacy risks of always-on cameras in XR glasses.
quiz.a: Recording bystanders without consent; collecting images of private spaces such as homes or offices.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is testing metaverse-ready factory twins and remote assistance on 5G edge nodes. Research is working on neural rendering and foveated streaming to cut bandwidth. Standards work continues on anchors and scene understanding in OpenXR. Search for 'OpenXR spatial anchors', 'WebXR hit test', and 'edge rendering motion-to-photon' to go deeper.
